wikipedia.title: Sandae-nori
categories: National Intangible Cultural Heritage of South Korea

profile.name: Sandae noli
profile.tagline: Korean mask dance drama managed by the Sandae Dogam until the early 1600s.
profile.insight: Disbanded in the early 1600s, the Sandae Dogam left performers jobless, shaping modern Korean plays like Yangju Byeolsandae.
profile.profile: Sandae-nori is a regional variant of Korean mask dance drama classified as a theatrical genre and a type of Korean dance. It was originally created and managed by the Sandae Dogam, a government office responsible for providing entertainment in the capital and important regional centers. Following the disbandment of this government office in the early 1600s, unemployed performers scattered and their stories influenced modern plays. Today, scholars view it as a potential root form for numerous Korean mask dance dramas.
profile.profile_long:
Sandae-nori, also written as Sandae noli, stands as a prominent regional variant of Korean mask dance drama. According to historical understanding and scholarly research, this performance genre holds a foundational place within the broader landscape of Korean dance traditions. Wikidata classifies the entity broadly as both a type of dance and a theatrical genre, specifically functioning as a subclass of Korean dance. Its historical significance is deeply intertwined with the administrative structures of early Korea, specifically through its governance and management.

The primary institutional driver behind Sandae-nori was the Sandae Dogam. This specialized government office was tasked with providing entertainment both in the capital city and across various important regional centers. Because of this official oversight and centralization, some scholars propose that Sandae-nori served as the root form for many other Korean mask dance dramas that exist today. The organized nature of the Sandae Dogam allowed the theatrical genre to maintain a high level of institutional support, structuring performances across different geographic regions of the country.

However, this centralized arrangement underwent a major disruption in the early 1600s. During this period, the Sandae Dogam was officially disbanded. This administrative dismantling left many performers entirely unemployed and forced them to travel in search of work. As these displaced artists integrated into new communities and shared their craft, their stories and performance techniques adapted. It is widely thought by researchers that the narratives and theatrical methods of these displaced performers evolved into modern-day plays such as Songpasandae-nori and Yangju Byeolsandae. Furthermore, this diaspora of talent exerted a lasting influence on many other performance forms across Korea.

In contemporary discussions of Korean performing arts, terminology often sparks confusion among modern audiences and outsiders. Modern Koreans frequently use the generic term 'talchum' to refer comprehensively to all types of mask dance dramas. Despite this widespread colloquial usage, academic and historical standards dictate that the term 'talchum' is properly applied only to three specific extant mask dance dramas originating from Hwanghae Province in North Korea. Understanding Sandae-nori requires recognizing this distinction, separating the broader umbrella of mask dance from the precise historical lineage of the Sandae Dogam and its descendant regional plays.

sections.origins_and_history: Sandae-nori is a regional variant of Korean mask dance drama. According to some scholars, it may be the root form of many other Korean mask dance dramas today, as it was created and managed by the Sandae Dogam, a government office in charge of providing entertainment both in the capital and in important regional centers. The Sandae Dogam was disbanded in the early 1600s, leaving many performers unemployed and searching for work. It is thought that the stories of these performers became modern day plays such as Songpasandae-nori and Yangju Byeolsandae and influenced many other performance forms in Korea.
